questions.knowledge_point: Integrating Products Containing the Exponential Function
questions.worked_solution:
Let's introduce the new variable $u=5-2{x}^{3}.$ Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-6{x}^{2}\,⟹\,-\text{d}u=6{x}^{2}\text{d}x.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 6{x}^{2}{e}^{5-2{x}^{3}}\,\text{d}x & =\int {e}^{5-2{x}^{3}}\cdot 6{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int {e}^{u}\cdot \,(-\text{d}u) \\  & =-\int {e}^{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-{e}^{u}+C \\  & =-{e}^{5-2{x}^{3}}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
Notice that the numerator is proportional to the derivative of the denominator. So, we introduce the new variable $u={5}^{x}+1.$ Differentiating gives 

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}={5}^{x}\operatorname{ln}⁡5\,⟹\,\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡5}\,\text{d}u={5}^{x}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{{5}^{x}}{{5}^{x}+1}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{{5}^{x}+1}\cdot {5}^{x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{u}\cdot \frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡5}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡5}\int \frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡5}\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡|u|+C \\  & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡5}\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡|{5}^{x}+1|+C \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡({5}^{x}+1)}{\operatorname{ln}⁡5}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that, in the last step, we used the fact that ${5}^{x}+1>0$ for all $x.$

$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {2}^{x+1}\sqrt{{2}^{x}-5}\,\text{d}x & =\int 2\cdot {2}^{x}\sqrt{{2}^{x}-5}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\int \sqrt{{2}^{x}-5}\cdot {2}^{x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\int \sqrt{u}\cdot \frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{2}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\int {u}^{1/2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{2}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\cdot \frac{{u}^{3/2}}{(\frac{3}{2})}+C \\  & =\frac{2}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\cdot \frac{2}{3}\cdot {u}^{3/2} \\  & =\frac{4}{3\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\sqrt{{u}^{3}}+C \\  & =\frac{4}{3\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\sqrt{({2}^{x}-5)^{3}}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Evaluating Definite Integrals
questions.worked_solution:
Let's introduce the new variable $u=2x+1.$ Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2\,⟹\,\text{d}u=2\,\text{d}x.
$$

Next, we determine the new limits of integration:

| $x$ | $0$ | $1$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $1$ | $3$ |

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}2\cdot {3}^{2x+1}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{1}^{3}{3}^{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & ={\frac{{3}^{u}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)}\,|}_{1}^{3} \\  & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)}({3}^{3}-{3}^{1}) \\  & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)}(27-3) \\  & =\frac{24}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Evaluating Definite Integrals
questions.worked_solution:
Let's introduce the new variable $u=3{e}^{x}+1.$ Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=3{e}^{x}\,⟹\,\text{d}u=3{e}^{x}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Next, we determine the new limits of integration:

| $x$ | $\operatorname{ln}⁡2$ | $\operatorname{ln}⁡5$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $7$ | $16$ |

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡5}\frac{12{e}^{x}}{3{e}^{x}+1}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡5}\frac{4}{3{e}^{x}+1}\cdot 3{e}^{x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{7}^{16}\frac{4}{u}\cdot \,\text{d}u \\  & =4{\int }_{7}^{16}\frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =4\operatorname{ln}⁡|u|\,{|}_{7}^{16} \\  & =4(\operatorname{ln}⁡(16)-\operatorname{ln}⁡(7)) \\  & =4\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{16}{7}).\end{aligned}
$$

Let's introduce the new variable $u = x^3+1.$ Differentiating gives

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}= 3x^2\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\dfrac 1 3 \textrm{d}u = x^2 \, \textrm{d}x.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {x}^{2}{e}^{{x}^{3}+1}\,\text{d}x & =\int {e}^{{x}^{3}+1}\cdot \,{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int {e}^{u}\cdot \frac{1}{3}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\int {e}^{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{e}^{u}+C \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{e}^{{x}^{3}+1}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Let's introduce the new variable $u= 1-x^4.$ Differentiating gives 

$$
\dfrac{ \textrm{d}u}{ \textrm{d}x} = -4x^3\quad\Longrightarrow\quad x^3 \, \textrm{d}x = -\dfrac{1}{4} \textrm{d}u.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\eqalign{
\int {x^3\,{3^{1-x^4}} }\, \textrm{d}x 
&=\int {{3^{1-x^4}}\cdot x^3 }\, \textrm{d}x \[5pt]
&=  \int {3^{u}} \cdot \left(-\dfrac{1}{4}\right) \textrm{d}u\[5pt]
                                                     &= -\dfrac{1}{4}\int {3^{u}}  \textrm{d}u\[5pt]
                                                     &=  -\dfrac{1}{4}\cdot\dfrac{3^{u}}{\ln 3} + C\[5pt]
                                                     &=   -\dfrac{3^{1-x^4}}{4\ln 3}+ C.
}
$$

Notice that the numerator is proportional to the derivative of the denominator. So, we introduce the new variable $u = e^{2x}+1.$ Differentiating gives 

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}= 2e^{2x}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\dfrac{1}{2}\, \textrm{d}u = e^{2x} \, \textrm{d}x.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{{e}^{2x}}{{e}^{2x}+1}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{{e}^{2x}+1}\cdot {e}^{2x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{u}\cdot \frac{1}{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡|u|+C \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡|{e}^{2x}+1|+C \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{2x}+1)+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that, in the last step, we used the fact that $e^{2x} + 1 > 0$ for all $x.$

Let's introduce the new variable $u=-2x^2.$ Differentiating gives

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}=-4x
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
-4 \, \textrm{d}u=16x \, \textrm{d}x.
$$

Next, we determine the new limits of integration:

| $x$ | $0$ | $\sqrt {\ln 4}$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $0$ | $-2\ln 4$ |

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{\operatorname{ln}⁡4}}16x{e}^{-2{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{\operatorname{ln}⁡4}}{e}^{-2{x}^{2}}\cdot 16x\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{-2\operatorname{ln}⁡4}{e}^{u}\cdot (-4\,\text{d}u) \\  & =-4{\int }_{0}^{-2\operatorname{ln}⁡4}{e}^{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-4{e}^{u}\,{|}_{0}^{-2\operatorname{ln}⁡4} \\  & =-4({e}^{-2\operatorname{ln}⁡4}-{e}^{0}) \\  & =-4(\frac{1}{16}-1) \\  & =4(\frac{15}{16}) \\  & =\frac{15}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$
